title: EHS Short Track Boots: How to Size, Fit and Heat Mould Them Properly
thumbnail_text: Short track boots: size, fit and heat mould

scenes.heading: Short Track Boots That Actually Fit
scenes.sub: Size, fit and heat mould your boots once, properly
scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you will know how to measure your feet, pick the right short track boot size, and heat mould the boot so it fits your foot. You will also know how to check the mould over your first three sessions. A high end short track boot only works when it fits. Get it right and the boot disappears under you. Get it wrong and you spend your season fighting lace bite, heel lift and numb toes instead of chasing lap times. Fit in this sport is a craft, not a shoe size.

scenes.heading: Why a short track boot is different
bullets: Built to lock one foot position
Rigid carbon shell resists twisting
Heel is the anchor for every push
Not running shoe logic
scenes.narration: A short track boot is not a stiffer fitness skate. It is a different tool. Short track means deep lean angles, hard crossovers and corners that never let go. The boot has to hold your ankle in one position and pass a sideways push straight into the blade. The EHS boot does this with a carbon fibre shell that refuses to twist when you load a corner. It is also built on a last made for short track, which supports your ankle and keeps your heel stable. That heel matters most. If the heel moves, your push leaks energy. Running shoe logic does not apply here.

scenes.heading: Measure your feet properly
bullets: Measure at the end of the day
Stand, heel against a wall
Measure both feet, use the larger
Measure width across the ball too
scenes.narration: Measure at the end of the day, when your feet are at their largest. Stand up, with weight on the foot. Put a sheet of paper against a wall, stand with your heel touching the wall, and mark the tip of your longest toe. That distance in millimetres is your working number. Measure both feet. Work from the larger one. Then measure the width across the ball of your foot, at its widest point. Width is where most fit problems live. A broad forefoot in a boot sized only on length will feel pressure on the outside of the foot within ten minutes. A narrow foot will find the heel floating, however hard you pull the laces.

scenes.heading: Where the boot should grip
scenes.narration: So how snug is snug? This diagram shows the three zones. At the back, the heel is locked. Across the middle, the midfoot is firm. At the front, your toes just brush the end when you stand upright, and pull back off it when you bend into a skating position. There should be no gap around the heel. If you can lift your heel more than a couple of millimetres with the boot laced, the boot is too big or the wrong shape for you. Many skaters buy half a size too large, because a properly fitted boot feels alarming in the shop. Resist that. A boot with room in it feels great for a week, then costs you a whole season of clean edges.

scenes.heading: Between sizes? Go smaller
bullets: Snug boots settle after moulding
Large boots never get smaller
Juniors: do not buy a size up
Unsure? Send your measurements first
scenes.narration: If you are between two sizes, take the smaller one, as long as your toes are not jammed against the front while standing. A slightly snug boot settles after moulding. A slightly large boot never gets smaller. The same rule applies to growing juniors. A boot bought a size large teaches bad technique. The skater grips with the toes to make up for the loose heel, and the foot is never really connected to the blade. Taking the smaller size and accepting a shorter service life is the better trade. And if your numbers do not sit neatly in one size, send your measurements to the shop before you order rather than guessing.

scenes.heading: Heat moulding in four steps
scenes.narration: Heat moulding turns a very good boot into your boot. The carbon shell can be warmed until it softens, laced onto your foot, then left to cool into your shape. Here are the four steps. One, warm the shell. Two, lace it onto your foot. Three, hold a skating posture with the knee driven forward, because moulding while standing relaxed gives you a boot shaped for standing, not skating. Four, let it cool fully before you take it off. Wear the exact socks you race in. And do not over tighten the laces while the shell cools. You want it to take your shape, not to be crushed into a shape that only works at full lace tension.

scenes.heading: Use a fitter for your first mould
bullets: Overheating can damage the shell
Follow the boot's own instructions
Home ovens and dryers are hard to control
Every heat cycle costs the shell a little
scenes.narration: If you have never moulded a carbon boot, have someone experienced do it. Overheating a carbon shell can damage the resin for good, and there is no undo. A good fitter controls the temperature and the time, gets the boot onto your foot quickly, holds your foot in a skating position while it cools, and checks the result. For temperature and time, follow the instructions that come with your boot. Do not guess from a video of a different brand. Hair dryers and home ovens are hard to control. A second mould is possible if the first is not right, but every heat cycle is a small cost to the shell. So treat the first attempt seriously.

scenes.heading: Shape, not size
scenes.chapter: What moulding can and cannot fix
scenes.narration: This is the most important idea in the whole guide. Moulding is a shape tool, not a size tool. On the left is what moulding can change. It can make room around an ankle bone, over a high instep, or at a bunion. And it can improve how closely the heel cup wraps your heel, which is the most valuable thing it does, because heel hold is where power is won or lost. On the right is what moulding cannot change. It cannot make the boot longer or shorter. It cannot shrink a shell that is too roomy. It cannot add a full width grade or fix the wrong last. Those are sizing problems. If the length or the basic shape is wrong, the answer is a different boot, not more heat.

scenes.heading: Read your first three sessions
bullets: Session one: twenty minutes, find sharp spots
Session two: note where and when
Session three: judge the heel
Home check: heel pinned, toes pull back
scenes.chapter: Checking the mould on the ice
scenes.narration: A mould is not finished when the boot comes off your foot. It is finished when three sessions on the ice confirm it. First, check at home. Lace up and stand. Your heel should feel pinned, with no lift when you rise onto the ball of your foot. Drop into a skating position. Your toes should pull back slightly, and nothing should bite across the top of the foot. Then go to the ice. In session one, skate only twenty minutes. Look for sharp local pain, not general stiffness. In session two, note where and when any discomfort shows up. In session three, push properly and judge the heel. If it lifts on a hard push, or your foot slides forward in the corner, that is a volume problem.

scenes.heading: Reading the boot after a mould
scenes.narration: Most complaints after a mould fall into four patterns. One sharp spot usually means a bony area the shell did not clear. The fix is local relief with controlled heat on that spot, not a full remould. Heel lifting means too much volume for your foot. Check your lacing first, then check the size. Pain across the top of the foot comes from lace pressure at the flex point. Relax the laces at the top and keep them firm over the midfoot. Numb toes mean compression, often from a shell that cooled with the laces pulled too hard. This is the one symptom you act on straight away. Loosen the lacing first. If that does not solve it, stop and have the boot checked before your next session.

scenes.heading: Living with the boot
bullets: Short sessions before full intervals
Thin race socks, never thick ones
Mounting cups are a separate purchase
Dry the boots after every session
scenes.narration: A well moulded carbon boot does not need a long, painful break in, but it does need a sensible start. Skate a few shorter sessions before a full interval set. If the boot feels tight, do not reach for thick socks. They fill the space the shell was moulded to leave for your foot. Mould in your race socks, then skate in those same socks. Remember that a short track skate is three parts. The boot bolts to a pair of mounting cups, and the cups hold the blade. The cups are a separate purchase, so budget for them. And dry your boots properly after every session, so the fit lasts for seasons, not months.

scenes.heading: Moulding fixes shape, not size
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: Here is the short version. Measure your feet properly. Take the snug size. Get the boot moulded by someone experienced. Remember that moulding fixes shape, not size. Then check the mould over your first three sessions, while small corrections are still easy. Do those things and the boot will feel like part of your leg rather than something you are wearing. The full guide on the LiveLica blog covers lacing, mounting cups, blade choice and a long list of common questions. The link is in the description.
